Introduction
Intravenous fluid resuscitation is a life-saving interven -
tion in critically ill patients with shock. It is one of the 
most common therapeutic interventions in critical care 
but often contributes to a degree of fluid accumulation, 
especially in conditions associated with oliguria or capil -
lary leak [1]. When the acute condition improves, most 
patients usually eliminate the accumulated fluids sponta -
neously during the recovery phase.
However, fluid accumulation may persist and contrib -
ute to harm. Moreover, sicker patients are more likely to 
receive larger volumes of fluid and are also more likely 
to die. The impact of fluid accumulation varies depend -
ing on age, comorbidity, and phase of illness but includes 
adverse consequences. It may induce pulmonary edema, 
prolonged mechanical ventilation, and development of 
acute kidney injury (AKI) but also delayed wound heal -
ing, tissue breakdown, and impaired bowel function 
with intestinal edema and intra-abdominal hypertension 
[2–4].
Fluid accumulation is a continuum and not defined by 
a specific threshold of fluid balance alone [5]. Clinicians 
concerned about the potential harm resulting from fluid 
accumulation may consider two solutions: (i) reducing/
restricting the volume of fluid administered to patients, 
and/or (ii) actively accelerating the removal of accumu -
lated fluid.

In critically ill adults who no longer require fluid resuscitation, does active acceleration of fluid removal, compared to usual care, improve 
patient important clinical outcomes?
PICO Description
Population Critically ill adults who no longer require fluid resuscitation (inclusion of 
critically ill patients in the ICU or emergency department and patients after 
major surgery; exclusion of chronic dialysis patients, patients with burns or 
diabetic ketoacidosis, pregnant women, and non‑ICU patients)
Intervention Active acceleration of fluid removal (using diuretics and/or ultrafiltration/RRT)
Comparator Usual care
Outcomes 1. Short‑term mortality
2. Quality of life
3. Physical function (e.g., activities of daily living)
4. Cognitive function
5. ICU‑free days
6. Hospital‑free days
7. ventilator‑free days
8. Need for RRT 
9. Development of AKI
Subgroups:
• Sepsis/septic shock
• Acute congestive heart failure
• Renal failure (acute/chronic)
• Acute hypoxic respiratory failure receiving respiratory support
• Different age groups
